issues.detail: Covers mostly the happy path and gives no guidance on missing data, ambiguous constraints, multiple candidate bottlenecks, or when the frameworks don't apply.
Framework sections such as Gall's Law, resilience vs optimization and the second-order tables restate well-known concepts at length.
Mostly conceptual framework descriptions with no step-by-step procedure for how the agent should gather data, run the analysis and structure its output.

scenarios.name: diagnose-slow-agency-delivery
scenarios.rationale: B explicitly walks through all five Focusing Steps (identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, repeat) and adds a dedicated second-order section covering the constraint moving, quality drift and single-point-of-failure, while A identifies the constraint and gives good fixes but never names the framework or steps and only implicitly covers the next constraint.

scenarios.name: feedback-loops-subscription-box-churn
scenarios.rationale: Both lay out explicit cause-effect loops; A labels reinforcing vs balancing more properly, includes a balancing loop, and gives a priority order, but its self-serve intervention is partial; B names self-serve help center/in-app credit as the weakest-link break and a strengthening flywheel, but mislabels loops as 'negative' and leaves the strengthen/break choice less explicit.

scenarios.name: evaluate-automate-all-support-and-discount
scenarios.rationale: Both reject doing both moves and propose phased automation with human escalation, but B explains the hard-edge-case problem more concretely (billing disputes, bugs, angry customers need humans) and keeps a 2–3 person escalation team, while A names the automation paradox, offers a free-tier/trial alternative and traces a loop, yet neither runs a clean first/second/third-order analysis and B's discount alternatives (shallower, time-boxed) are less aligned with the rubric's free-tier suggestion.
